questions.question: During the colonial period, how did 'enrichment plantations' damage forest biodiversity in India?
options: A single commercially valuable tree species was extensively planted, systematically eliminating other natural forest species (e.g. Teak in South India and Chir Pine in the Himalayas)
They covered all forests with concrete
They poisoned all natural freshwater streams
questions.explanation: Colonial 'scientific forestry' prioritized timber profits: single commercial species like Teak monocultures in South India or Chir Pine in the Himalayas displaced diverse natural broadleaved ecosystems.

questions.question: According to the Forest Survey of India, between 1951 and 1980, how much forest land was converted into agricultural land across the country?
questions.explanation: Between 1951 and 1980, more than 26,200 sq km of pristine forest was cleared and cleared for agricultural expansion across India.

questions.question: The construction of the Narmada Sagar Project in Madhya Pradesh submerged approximately how many hectares of forest land?
questions.explanation: Clearing forests for river valley projects has been devastating: the Narmada Sagar multipurpose project alone inundated 40,000 hectares of forest in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.question: The Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal is seriously threatened by which ongoing extractive activity?
questions.explanation: The Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal faces severe ecological degradation and fragmentation of elephant migration corridors due to ongoing dolomite mining.

questions.question: Ecological studies show that in Indian society, the richest 5 percent cause significantly more environmental damage than the poorest 25 percent because:
options: The richest 5% consume vastly more energy, minerals, and manufactured goods per capita while bearing almost no direct responsibility for environmental degradation
The poor use more aeroplanes than the rich
The rich live exclusively inside national parks
The poor control all industrial corporations
questions.explanation: High per capita consumption of fossil fuels, industrial goods, and luxury transport by the wealthy elite drives resource extraction and pollution, far exceeding the ecological footprint of rural poor.

questions.question: In impoverished rural communities, why does deforestation and environmental degradation affect women more severely than men?
options: Women bear the primary responsibility of collecting fuel, fodder, water, and basic subsistence needs, forcing them to walk over 10 km daily as resources deplete
Women are legally prohibited from entering forests
Only men are allowed to collect water from rivers
Women work exclusively in steel factories
questions.explanation: In rural households, women gather fuelwood, water, and fodder. Forest destruction increases their drudgery, requiring walks of 10+ kilometers, impacting their health and causing neglect of home and children.

questions.question: In Rajasthan's Sariska Tiger Reserve, local villagers successfully fought against marble and dolomite mining by:
options: Citing the provisions of the Wildlife Protection Act and challenging miners in courts and on the ground
questions.explanation: Villagers around Sariska Tiger Reserve organized grassroots resistance, actively citing the Wildlife Protection Act to stop destructive commercial mining in the reserve's buffer zones.

questions.question: In and around the villages of the Bishnoi community in Rajasthan, herds of which wild animals are seen roaming freely and protected as integral members of the community?
questions.explanation: Bishnoi religious precepts mandate strict protection of all animal and plant life. Herds of blackbuck, nilgai, and peacocks live safely amidst Bishnoi settlements.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Geography, Chapter 2, Section 4, Box

questions.question: Which of the following are examples of critically endangered wild plant species in India that are on the verge of extinction?
options: Madhuca insignis (a wild mahua) and Hubbardia heptaneuron (a grass species)
questions.explanation: Madhuca insignis (a wild variety of mahua) and Hubbardia heptaneuron (a unique grass species growing near waterfalls) are among the most critically endangered wild flora in India.

questions.question: According to the IUCN categories, which of the following animals is classified under the 'Vulnerable' category?
questions.explanation: Vulnerable species include the Gangetic dolphin, Asiatic elephant, and blue sheep, whose numbers have depleted and will slide into the endangered category if threats persist.

questions.question: In which year were plants added to the protected species list under the Indian Wildlife Act for the first time, starting with six species?
questions.explanation: In 1991, for the very first time, plants were included under the protected species list of the Wildlife Act, with six rare botanical species granted legal protection.

questions.question: Species with small global populations that can move into the endangered or vulnerable category if negative factors continue operating are categorized as:
questions.explanation: Rare species (like the Himalayan brown bear, wild Asiatic buffalo, and hornbill) naturally possess small populations, making them highly vulnerable to sudden environmental pressures.

questions.question: Why are Reserved and Protected forests collectively referred to as 'Permanent Forest Estates'?
options: They are maintained by the state for the purpose of producing timber and other forest produce, and for protective reasons to safeguard ecological balance
They can never be visited by any human being
They are permanently exempt from all rainfall
They are leased permanently to multinational pharmaceutical companies
questions.explanation: Permanent Forest Estates (reserved + protected) represent government-controlled forest lands managed perpetually for timber yield, watershed preservation, and wildlife habitats.

questions.subtopic: Khasi and Jaintia Hills Sacred Groves
questions.question: The sacred groves of which state are described by botanists as the last remaining refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plant species?
questions.explanation: The pristine sacred groves preserved by the Khasi and Jaintia tribes in Meghalaya contain ancient, undisturbed climax forests that preserve critically endangered endemic plants.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Geography, Chapter 2, Section 4, Box

questions.question: Substantial parts of the tribal belts in north-eastern and central India have been deforested or degraded by:
options: Shifting cultivation (jhum), a type of slash-and-burn agriculture
questions.explanation: Shifting cultivation (jhum) practiced across tribal highlands involves cutting and burning forest plots, leading to severe forest fragmentation when fallow cycles are shortened.

questions.question: During weddings, the tribal communities of Odisha and Bihar revere and worship which trees as part of their sacred marriage rituals?
questions.explanation: Tribal peoples of Odisha and Bihar worship tamarind and mango trees during marriage rituals, demonstrating traditional cultural bonds with floral species.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Geography, Chapter 2, Section 4, Box

questions.question: What are the major threats to the tiger population that necessitated the launch of Project Tiger in India?
options: Poaching for tiger skins and bones used in traditional medicines, habitat shrinkage, and depletion of prey base
Competition from domestic cattle for pasture grass
questions.explanation: Commercial poaching for tiger skins and traditional East Asian medicinal bones, along with relentless habitat destruction and decline in prey animals (deer, boar), pushed tigers to the brink.

questions.question: In which northeastern state is the famous Manas Tiger Reserve and Biosphere Reserve located?
questions.explanation: Manas Tiger Reserve is located in Assam, nestled in the foothills of the Himalayas, renowned for tigers, pygmy hogs, and wild water buffaloes.

questions.question: The critically endangered 'Sangai' (brow-antlered deer) is endemic to which unique wetland national park in India?
options: Keibul Lamjao National Park on Loktak Lake in Manipur
questions.explanation: The Sangai (dancing deer) is endemic exclusively to the floating phumdis of Keibul Lamjao National Park on Loktak Lake in Manipur.

questions.subtopic: Genetic Diversity in Fisheries and Crops
questions.question: Why is the preservation of biodiversity crucial for the future of human agriculture and fisheries?
options: It preserves the genetic diversity of wild relatives essential for breeding disease-resistant crops and robust aquatic species
It ensures all crops grow without sunlight
It allows all marine fish to live in freshwater lakes
It prevents rivers from flowing into oceans
questions.explanation: Wild plant and animal strains contain unique genetic traits that agricultural scientists use to breed drought-tolerant, pest-resistant hybrid crops and sustain healthy fishery stocks.
